analysis.one_liner: Makes companies liable for discrimination by their AI decision systems and funds federal bias testing.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors in the Senate's final 13 days, the bill died in committee without ever getting a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make clear that a company or agency using artificial intelligence to decide who gets a job, loan, apartment, or benefit is legally responsible if that decision discriminates — exactly as if a human had made it. It would also create a temporary program at the National Institute of Standards and Technology to test AI systems for bias based on race, sex, age, disability, and other protected traits, with the program ending after 2028.
analysis.who_benefits: People on the receiving end of automated decisions — job applicants, borrowers, renters, benefits recipients, and voters — who could hold companies and agencies liable when an AI system discriminates against them, and who would benefit from a federal program identifying bias in tools like facial recognition and credit recommendation systems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People judged by AI hiring, lending, and housing tools

how_it_helps.text: Would make a company or agency using AI to make or inform a decision legally liable for discrimination under civil rights laws in the same manner and to the same extent as if the entity had made the decision without AI — so algorithmic tools could not be used as a loophole around existing protections.

Would apply across a wide range of protections — race, sex, age, disability, genetic information, employment, housing, voting, and benefits — including federal, state, and local anti-discrimination laws, so the clarification covers decisions made by employers, lenders, agencies, and others.

Would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to run evaluations of AI systems for bias, prioritizing high-risk uses like facial and gait recognition, speech recognition, and recommendation systems in finance and criminal justice, and to help entities mitigate what the tests find.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that develop or deploy AI decision systems — software vendors, employers, lenders, landlords, insurers, and agencies — would bear liability for discriminatory outcomes and the cost of bias testing and mitigation. Taxpayer funds would cover the standards program through 2028.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tech vendors and businesses using AI decision tools

drawbacks.text: The bill bans nothing. The NIST bias evaluations would be voluntary and advisory — the program assesses and 'assists in mitigating' bias rather than requiring anyone to fix or stop using a biased system — and the whole program sunsets on December 31, 2028.

The definition of artificial intelligence is very broad — any data system or software using machine learning 'in whole or in part' — so ordinary businesses using common automated tools could face added litigation uncertainty over decisions that were already covered by civil rights law.
Funding is left open-ended ('such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal 2023 through 2028) rather than specifying or capping what the evaluations program would cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The help it offered was real but modest. The bill changed no rules about what AI may do; it confirmed that existing civil rights law already applies to algorithmic decisions and set up a voluntary, temporary testing program. That would have given people a clearer path to challenge biased automated decisions in hiring, lending, housing, and benefits. The costs fall on businesses using AI tools — liability they arguably already faced under existing law, plus uncertainty from the bill's sweeping AI definition. A stronger version would have required bias audits instead of merely running voluntary evaluations.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate's last days and sent to committee, and the Congress ended before any hearing, markup, or vote could happen.

narrative.text: Senator Rob Portman introduced the bill on December 21, 2022 — thirteen days before the 117th Congress ended — with no cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which never took it up.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that sell and use AI decision tools are better off, since they face no new civil rights liability or federal bias evaluations. For the people the bill aimed to protect from algorithmic discrimination, nothing changed.

for.name: Sen. Rob Portman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the Senate's final working days; no colleague joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Maria Cantwell, D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 21, 2022 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsored it, no one from either party signed on, and no vote was ever held, so partisan alignment was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would hold anyone deploying an AI system liable for discriminatory outcomes as if a human made the decision, and would subject tools like facial recognition and speech systems to federal bias evaluations. Their interest in avoiding liability and scrutiny runs against the people those tools judge.

industries.industry: Employers, lenders, and insurers using automated decision tools
industries.note: Hiring, credit, insurance, and benefits decisions made or informed by algorithms would carry the same civil rights liability as human decisions, and covered entities' systems would be evaluated for bias. Cheaper automated screening could no longer quietly shift discrimination risk onto applicants and borrowers.

Sensitive image recognition, including facial and gait recognition, was a named priority for the bias evaluation program, and recommendation systems used in criminal justice would also be assessed. These sectors would face federal testing of products whose errors fall hardest on protected groups.
